e.t: This word means “favorite slave.” It is a noun or adjective describing a slave who holds a favored or specially valued place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, appearing in Genesis, Exodus, and Esther. Its use in Esther is especially frequent, while its occurrences in Genesis and Exodus show that the term belongs to ordinary descriptions of household or court servants. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone who is loved or beloved. It identifies a person as dearly valued and cherished, whether in a family relationship or in another setting where affection and honor are expressed. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 20 times, including several occurrences in Psalms and Genesis. Its basic sense remains consistent: the person described is the object of love. The surrounding verse determines who is being called beloved and what relationship or situation gives that description its particular force.

This adjective describes someone or something as “high-minded” or “lordly”—elevated in character, bearing, or status. It presents a sense of nobility or commanding dignity rather than merely describing physical height. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 1:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense points to an elevated, dignified, or princely quality.

Azarael, also rendered Azarel, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament’s rendering of 1 Chronicles. The name occurs twice in this corpus, in 1 Chronicles 25:4 and 1 Chronicles 27:22. Without the surrounding verse text, these references establish where the name appears but do not provide further meaning or a description of the person.

Aialōn is a proper name, rendered “Aialōn” or “Ealon.” It identifies a named place or person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Chronicles 11:10. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the specific role of the name in that passage cannot be stated more precisely. Its basic meaning is therefore its function as a distinct biblical name.

This adjective means “wanting the heart,” describing someone or something as lacking the heart or inner quality needed for a matter. It appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus: three times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense remains a deficiency connected with the heart. The word occurs in Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Sirach.

This adjective describes something done against a person’s will—something involuntary rather than freely chosen. It can refer to an action or circumstance that happens without deliberate consent. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs four times, including three occurrences in Numbers and one in Ecclesiastes. Its central sense remains consistent: the matter is not intentional or willingly accepted. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This noun means “anything heard with pleasure”—something listened to because it is enjoyable or pleasing to hear. It refers broadly to an appealing sound, speech, song, or other auditory delight, without identifying a particular kind of sound by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 32:4. Its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains something received with enjoyment through hearing.

This word describes someone or something as “sinning.” As a noun or adjective, it can name a person or characterize what is being described as sinning. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 2 and 3 Maccabees. The word itself supplies this basic description, while the surrounding passage provides the fuller sense of its use in each occurrence.

Allōēs is a proper name referring to a person named Alloes, also rendered Allis. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Nehemiah 3:12. The name’s precise significance or the person’s role cannot be determined from the name alone; the surrounding verse and passage are needed for that. Its basic function is simply to identify an individual.

This Greek LXX verb means to stay up for someone or something, or to wait. It describes remaining in expectation rather than leaving or giving up. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scriptures represented here, including passages from Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its use can therefore cover both patient waiting and actively staying awake for an expected person or event. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This LXX Greek verb expresses the idea of resting something in place or fixing it firmly. Its basic sense is “rest; fix,” so it can describe putting something down securely or establishing it where it belongs. It occurs five times in the Greek LXX, each in a different verse, showing a concise action word rather than a broad title or abstract concept. The exact force in any passage depends on what is being rested or fixed and on the surrounding sentence.

gl: reject from oneself; cast off from oneself
d: reject from oneself; cast off from oneself

e.t: This verb means to reject something or someone from oneself—to cast it away or refuse association. It describes an act of removal or repudiation rather than simple distance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in Job, where its repeated use concerns rejecting, casting off, or refusing something. The precise force in each sentence depends on what is being rejected and the surrounding context, but the central idea remains a deliberate turning away or casting off.citep03:word:lxx:L701552:identityp03:word:lxx:L701552:occurrences

This Greek LXX noun means “fastening”—something that joins or holds parts together. It describes a connecting or securing bond rather than an action performed by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not provided here. The word points to parts being brought into connection and held together. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX adjective means “male.” It describes a person or living creature as male, distinguishing male from female when that distinction matters in a passage. It is used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, appearing 60 times in this LXX corpus. The word commonly identifies male people, and its precise grammatical role is determined by the noun or person it describes. It does not by itself state anything beyond the basic distinction of sex.

This Greek LXX proper noun means “Askalonitēs” or “Askalonitis,” identifying an Askalonite—someone associated with Askalon. It functions as a name or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Joshua 13:3 and 1 Samuel 5:10. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise reference in each passage cannot be explained further, but its basic sense remains a designation connected with Askalon.

Asyber is a personal name, also rendered Asivir. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 26:42. The available wording identifies the name itself, but without the surrounding verse text it does not establish the person’s character, role, family significance, or the meaning of the passage. Its main function is simply to name a particular person in that genealogical setting.

This Greek verb means “spring off,” describing a sudden movement away from a place or position. It presents action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a quick departure or leaping away.

This LXX verb means to “distance” oneself or to “keep distance.” It describes moving away, withdrawing, or remaining apart rather than staying near. The central idea is separation, whether the word refers to a person leaving a place, people turning away, or something being kept at a distance. It occurs 199 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense is well established across many passages. The precise force in any verse depends on who or what is being separated.

This word means “reed-grass,” naming a plant rather than an action, quality, or person. It functions as a noun, so it identifies the grass itself when it appears in a sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Old Testament books and once in Sirach. Its basic meaning remains focused and specific: reed-grass, without requiring additional metaphorical or spiritual meaning apart from the surrounding verse.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Belisa” or “Velisa.” It identifies a person or name-bearing figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 47:14. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide the surrounding verse text, so its precise role in that passage cannot be described here. The two forms reflect approved renderings of the same name, not separate meanings.

This word means “antelope,” a noun naming a type of animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 14:5. The word identifies an animal included in the passage’s list of creatures; the surrounding verse supplies the specific context for how it is classified there. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: it refers to an antelope, rather than describing an action, quality, or person.

This Greek LXX noun means “depth” or “deep,” describing something far down or extending far below the surface. It is used as a noun, so it can name a deep place or depth rather than describe an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, all in six verses. English renderings use “depth” once and “deep” repeatedly, showing that the central idea remains great downward distance or profound depth. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Gimel is a noun whose meaning is the designation “Gimel,” rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Psalm 118:17. Its lexical meaning is simply the name “Gimel”; no additional sense or broader usage is established by the available information. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its specific role there.

This word means “is necessary” or “have to.” It expresses that something is required, unavoidable, or must take place. As a verb, it describes necessity rather than merely reporting that something happens. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 40 times across 37 verses, including passages in the Law, historical books, wisdom writings, and later Jewish Scriptures. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is said to be necessary and why, but its central idea remains clear: a requirement or obligation that cannot simply be treated as optional.

This adjective means “second”: it identifies a person, thing, or position that follows the first in an order or sequence. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly for the second item or occurrence in an arrangement, rather than naming a particular object by itself. The word occurs 206 times in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through 4 Maccabees, including descriptions of days, rows, offerings, and other ordered things.

This verb means “head through” or “lead.” It describes directing or bringing someone through a place, situation, or course of action. It can therefore refer either to guiding others or to causing something to pass through. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 21 times, so its central idea is consistent while the surrounding context determines who is being led and what path is involved.

gl: drive a nail through; nail fast
d: drive a nail through; nail fast

e.t: This verb means “drive a nail through” or “nail fast.” It describes the physical action of fastening something securely by driving a nail through it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both within Judges 5:26, so its known use is concentrated in one verse. The word expresses a direct, forceful fastening action rather than a general idea of securing or holding. Its precise force in that passage is understood more fully from the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to a trench or conduit: a channel made to carry or direct water. It can describe a dug passage, drainage channel, or watercourse rather than water itself. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, including passages associated with Egypt, rivers, and channels. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding description, but its central idea remains a constructed or defined passage through which water flows.

This adjective means “granted,” describing something given or allowed by another. It presents the matter as received through another person’s decision or favor, rather than as something claimed independently. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 1:11. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains that of something granted.

This adverb means “maliciously,” describing an action done with harmful or hostile intent. It tells how someone acts rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:11. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is conduct marked by deliberate ill will or a desire to cause harm.

This noun refers to an “odious look”—an appearance or expression that is repulsive, unpleasant, or offensive to see. It describes how someone or something is perceived by sight, focusing on the negative impression created by its appearance rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 16:3. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX verb means “lick up”: to consume or remove something by licking it. It describes the action of licking something until it is taken up, rather than merely touching it with the tongue. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Numbers and 1 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary sense remains direct and concrete: licking something up.

This noun means “mercy”: compassionate treatment shown toward someone who is needy, guilty, or dependent. It describes a disposition or action that does not simply demand what might be deserved, but responds with kindness and help. In the Greek Old Testament, the word is used across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, including Proverbs, Psalms, and Sirach. Its repeated use in wisdom writings highlights mercy as a quality closely associated with righteous living. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Eliakim is a personal name, also rendered Eliakeim. It identifies a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twelve times across twelve verses, appearing in 2 Kings, Isaiah, 2 Chronicles, and Nehemiah. Because it is a proper name, its meaning in any one passage comes from the person being identified and the surrounding account, not from the name functioning as an ordinary vocabulary term. The name appears in passages including 2 Kings 18:18 and 2 Chronicles 36:4.

Emmanouel, also rendered Emmanoïl, is a proper name rather than a general description or action. It identifies a person by name in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This word occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Isaiah 7:14. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its broader scriptural context, but the lexical role itself is straightforward: it functions as a personal name.

This Greek verb means “wear”: to have something on the body as clothing or an adornment. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its precise force depends on what is being worn in the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 14:44. The word’s central idea remains the act of wearing something.

This word means “habit”: a settled pattern or practice that becomes customary through repetition. As a noun in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it describes something established in a person’s conduct or way of life. It occurs 14 times in this corpus, showing that it can refer broadly to an accustomed practice rather than a single action. The surrounding verse determines what particular habit or established pattern is meant.

This verb means “lift up” or “exalt,” describing the act of raising someone or something to a higher position or honor. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 7:28. Its basic sense points to elevation, whether understood literally or as being given greater honor. The precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun means “prudence”: the careful, sensible judgment that helps a person think wisely and act appropriately. It describes practical discernment rather than mere knowledge, pointing to sound judgment in choosing words or actions. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 16:23, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains the ability to consider matters wisely and respond with measured understanding.

This Greek LXX verb means “stamp,” describing the action of pressing or striking the foot against the ground. It presents stamping as an active movement rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Ezekiel 25:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the physical action of stamping. This is a rare word in the LXX corpus, with no further occurrences recorded there.

Eseron is a proper name, referring to a person named Eseron rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears six times in the Greek Old Testament, all within the genealogical material of 1 Chronicles 2, across five verses. Its repeated use identifies the same named figure or figures within that family record, while the surrounding genealogy determines each specific relationship. The supplied material establishes the name and its occurrences, but does not provide a broader lexical meaning for it.

This Greek LXX noun means “companion”—someone associated with or accompanying another person. It presents the idea of a fellow associate rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, with one occurrence each in Judges, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its exact nuance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a companion or associate.

This adjective describes something that is easily destroyed or perishable. It points to a condition of being unable to last, emphasizing frailty and the likelihood of decay or ruin rather than permanence. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:21. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a clear description of what does not endure.

“Ephod” is the name of a specific biblical object. As a noun, this word identifies that object rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it appears nine times, all in 1 Samuel, showing a focused use within this corpus. The English rendering preserves the same term, “ephod,” rather than replacing it with a broader descriptive word.

Zaboulōn is a proper name, presented in the Greek Old Testament as “Zaboulōn” or “Zavulon.” It identifies the biblical name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This word occurs 46 times across 44 Old Testament verses, from Genesis through Ezekiel, so it is used repeatedly as a stable name throughout the biblical record. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a name.

This adverb means “stilly” or “quietly,” describing an action done in a calm, hushed, or undisturbed manner. It answers the question of how something happens rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Isaiah and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on silence, calmness, or stillness in that particular setting.

This noun means “defeat”—the condition or result of being overcome. It names a loss rather than describing the action of defeating someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 31:8, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic sense remains a reversal in which one side is overcome and does not prevail.

This noun means “room,” referring to a defined space or place within a building or structure. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 22 times, with many occurrences in Ezekiel, where descriptions of rooms and measured spaces are especially prominent. Its basic sense remains straightforward: an enclosed or designated area. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and what kind of space is being described.

Thimath is a proper name identifying a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. The name itself is rendered “Thimath,” so no broader ordinary meaning is established beyond this name. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 30:28. Its precise referent and significance depend on the surrounding verse and passage, since the name alone does not indicate whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity.

Iaaim, also given as Iaem, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 7:19. Because it functions as a proper name and no additional definition or contextual wording is provided here, its significance is identifying the person named rather than expressing a broader concept. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s place in the genealogy.

Iamin is a proper name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship; its meaning here is the personal designation “Iamin.” The name occurs ten times in ten Old Testament verses, appearing in genealogical and historical records from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. Its precise identity in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This verb means to win someone over—to gain that person’s acceptance, loyalty, or support. It describes an active effort to make another person one’s own ally rather than merely persuading someone about a single point. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 15:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on gaining another person’s favor and allegiance.

The word is a proper name for Jerusalem, expressed in this Greek form as “Ierosolymos; Ierosolimos.” It identifies the city rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 18 times, all in the Deuterocanonical writings, especially 2 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains the city’s name, while the surrounding verse shows what is being said about Jerusalem in each occurrence.

Iephthae is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears mainly in Judges and once in 1 Samuel, with 29 occurrences across 25 verses. The name is especially associated with the account in Judges 11, where the person named Iephthae is repeatedly mentioned. Its meaning is therefore primarily identifying: it names the individual, while the surrounding passage supplies what he does and why he is being discussed.

Iōsadak, also rendered Iosathak, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, in 1 Chronicles 5:40 and 5:41. The available form gives the person’s name but does not provide an additional meaning or definition for the name itself. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

This noun means “camel,” the large, hump-backed animal used for carrying people and goods. In the Greek Old Testament, it refers to camels as ordinary animals within accounts of travel, wealth, and household possessions. The word occurs 55 times across 51 verses, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Zechariah, showing that it is a familiar concrete term rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage and how the camel is being mentioned there.

This verb means “shame” or “put to shame”: it describes bringing disgrace upon someone or causing a person to be treated as dishonored. It can also express the experience of being shamed, depending on how the sentence uses the verb. In this Greek-scripture corpus, it occurs 73 times, so it is a recurring word for disgrace rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

The word is a verb meaning “dislodge” or “lodge”: it can describe removing someone or something from a place, or staying in a place for the night. These are two distinct uses of the same LXX Greek verb, so the surrounding sentence determines which sense is intended. It occurs 53 times in the LXX corpus represented here, including the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its basic idea concerns either departure from a lodging place or remaining as a guest.

This Greek verb means “curse”: to speak or call down harm upon someone or something. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 70 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures, and it also appears in deuterocanonical books. Its repeated use across historical, legal, poetic, and prophetic writings shows a broad action-word meaning centered on cursing. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

The word means “pray earnestly.” It is a verb describing prayer expressed with seriousness, intensity, and deliberate appeal. Its central idea is not simply to speak about prayer, but to engage in prayer with focused purpose. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage is best understood alongside the surrounding verse and passage.

This verb means “mix”: to combine things so that they are brought together. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Psalm 101:10, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains the joining or blending of separate things into a mixture.

This noun refers to lying down, and by extension to sexual relations. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it is used 70 times, especially in passages concerning bodily states, sexual conduct, and places of rest. Its basic sense can therefore describe the act or setting of lying down, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the reference is ordinary rest or intimate relations. The word appears from Genesis through Song of Songs, showing use across varied settings rather than a meaning limited to one subject.

This Greek LXX verb means “cast forth” or “throw out”—to send something away from oneself or remove it by force or deliberate action. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:15, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains the act of casting or driving something outward.

This Greek word means “take” or “get.” It is a verb describing the act of receiving, obtaining, picking up, or taking hold of something, depending on the sentence. It can refer to taking an object, receiving something given, obtaining a person or thing, or acquiring what is needed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 1,189 times, showing that it is a broad, ordinary action word rather than a term limited to one subject. Its precise sense in any verse is determined by what is being taken or received and by the surrounding wording.

Luza is a proper name for a place, rendered “Luza” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a descriptive word or title, so its meaning is primarily identification: it names a location mentioned in Israel’s history. The name occurs eight times in seven verses, in Genesis, Joshua, and Judges. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and place-related context, but the word itself functions as a geographic name rather than an ordinary vocabulary term.

This word is a proper name, identifying someone or something called “Maouek” or “Mauek.” It is not a general description or action word, but a particular name used in the Greek Old Testament. The word occurs once in the LXX, at Judges 6:26. Without the verse text and surrounding context, the name’s specific referent cannot be identified more precisely here.

This word means “honey,” the sweet food produced by bees and gathered or eaten as food. It is a noun naming a tangible substance, and its use in the Greek Old Testament includes descriptions of the land’s abundance, food, and desirable provisions. The word occurs 62 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its ordinary meaning remains consistent, while the surrounding passage determines how honey functions in a particular verse.

Misach is a personal name referring to one individual in the Greek Old Testament book of Daniel. It is not an ordinary descriptive word, action, or quality, but a proper name used to identify the same person throughout its occurrences. The name appears 11 times in the Greek LXX text, all within Daniel, from Daniel 1:7 through Daniel 3:97. Its precise significance in any verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This noun refers to “defilement” or “pollution,” identifying a condition in which someone or something has been made unclean. It describes the resulting state rather than necessarily naming the action that caused it. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, the word occurs once, at Jeremiah 51:4, so its wider range cannot be established from repeated uses in this corpus. Its precise application depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

gl: plug a wound with lint; bind up
d: plug a wound with lint; bind up

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “plug a wound with lint; bind up.” It describes the practical act of closing or dressing an injury so it can be cared for and healed. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In this LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Hosea 6:1, but the verse text is not available here, so its wider significance in that passage should be understood from the surrounding context. The basic picture is active care given to a wounded place.

This word describes something as “full of marrow,” referring to being filled with the rich inner substance of bone. As a verb, it expresses this condition rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 65:15, and its normal meaning remains focused on fullness of marrow. The exact force in that verse depends on its surrounding wording.

This adjective means “newly founded,” describing something that has recently been established or brought into being. It points to newness in the origin or establishment of a person, place, community, or thing, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Wisdom 11:18. Because the verse text is not included here, the word’s precise reference in that passage cannot be identified beyond its basic sense: something newly established rather than long-standing.

This LXX Greek noun means “disease,” referring to sickness that affects a person’s health. It is used as a naming word for an illness, whether mentioned generally or as a condition experienced by particular people. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, including several occurrences in Deuteronomy and 2 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any individual verse comes from that passage’s surrounding context.

This word means “sluggishness” or “laziness”—a lack of energy, diligence, or willingness to act. As a noun, it names this condition rather than describing a person directly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 10:18. Its basic sense points to neglectful inactivity, especially when needed work is left undone. The surrounding passage is needed to determine the precise force of the word in that verse, but its central idea remains a failure to apply oneself with needed care and effort.

This adjective means “of what kind,” and is used to ask about or identify the kind, nature, or character of something. It points beyond merely naming an object to the quality or category that distinguishes it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:37. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic function is to ask or describe what sort of thing is meant.

Ochozias is a proper name used in the Greek Septuagint, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also rendered “Okhozias,” giving two accepted English forms for the same source name. In this Old Testament corpus, it occurs 25 times across 24 verses, with most occurrences in 2 Kings. It appears from 1 Kings through 2 Chronicles.

This adverb means “in every way,” expressing completeness or an all-encompassing manner. It describes how something is done or understood without limiting the statement to one aspect. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in Sirach and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains comprehensive scope: something applies fully, broadly, or in every respect rather than only partially.

This Greek LXX verb means “preserve” or “acquire”: it describes keeping something safe or obtaining it. As an action word, it focuses on what someone does to secure, retain, or gain something. It occurs 29 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its precise sense is shaped by what is being preserved or acquired in each passage. The central idea remains active possession or protection rather than a mere inward desire.

This noun means “bitterness,” referring to a bitter quality or condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers, showing that its basic sense is a condition marked by bitterness rather than an action or person. The word appears in Numbers 33:8 and 33:9, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force in either passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an “organ of,” naming a bodily organ. Its basic sense identifies a physical part of the body rather than an action, quality, or person. The precise bodily reference in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the word itself points to an organ as a physical body part.

e.h: A Woman Who Is a Prostitute
e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “prostitute,” referring to a woman who engages in sexual relations for payment. It is a direct, concrete designation rather than a general description of sexual behavior. The word occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing that it is used across several kinds of passages, including narratives, laws, and prophetic writings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek verb means “provide”: to supply or make available what is needed. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it tells what someone does. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including Proverbs, Daniel, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “going up” or “ascent.” It describes upward movement or a rise from one place toward another, functioning as a name for that movement rather than an action word. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:3. The single occurrence identifies where the word appears, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force in that passage. Its basic sense remains movement upward.

This noun refers to an advantage or victory—the upper hand or success gained over another. It names a favorable outcome rather than an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Judges 4:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to gaining the better position or prevailing in a contest. Scripture’s use here presents the word as a term for the result or benefit of coming out ahead.

This Greek LXX noun means “fist,” referring to the hand considered as a physical object. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Exodus and once in Isaiah. The word names a bodily instrument or means of striking, but its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains concrete and physical rather than describing an emotion, idea, or spiritual quality.

Remmath is a proper name, referring to a specific place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it is rendered “Remmath” and appears eight times, all in eight verses. Most of these occurrences are in 1 Kings, with one in Joshua. Because it functions as a place name, its meaning is primarily identification: it names a location mentioned in the biblical account. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what happens there or why the place matters in that passage.

Saph is a personal name, also identified as Saf. It names an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this name occurs once, at 1 Kings 4:6. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide a separate definition or explain the person’s role. Its significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

Sesi is a proper name identifying a person. Its meaning is presented simply as “Sesi,” so it functions as a personal designation rather than a general description, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, in Ezra 10:40. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, the name itself does not establish the person’s role or significance beyond identifying that individual.

The word means “perversely,” describing an action or conduct that is contrary to what is right or proper. As an adverb, it tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 6:28; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force in that passage.

Sophonias is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used as the name Sophonias, also rendered Sofonias. The name occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages in 2 Kings, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Zechariah. Because it is a personal name, its basic meaning is its identification of a particular individual. The surrounding verse is needed to determine which person named Sophonias is meant in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “encampment”: a place where an army or organized group sets up camp. It refers to the camp itself rather than the act of camping. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical corpus, in Joshua 4:3 and 2 Maccabees 13:14. Its basic sense is therefore a settled military or group camp, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation being described.

This Greek LXX verb means “mix together” or “commingle”—to bring separate things or people into one combined setting. It describes the act of mingling rather than merely being near one another. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, from Exodus through 2 Maccabees, showing use across both narrative and wisdom writings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being joined and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “accustom.” It describes the action of causing someone or oneself to become accustomed to something, or the state of being accustomed through repeated practice. In the LXX, it occurs three times, all in Sirach 23:9, 23:13, and 23:15. Its central idea is developing a settled familiarity with something rather than describing a single, isolated action. The surrounding verse determines exactly what a person is being accustomed to in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “reconcile”: to bring opposing people or sides back into agreement. It describes an action of restoring peace or settling a conflict rather than merely recognizing that a disagreement exists. The word occurs three times, all in 2 Maccabees, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the available material does not include the surrounding verse text. Its precise force in any one passage depends on who is being brought together and what conflict is being addressed.

Sōson, also written Soson, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, object, or quality. Its meaning is therefore its use as a personal designation, and the surrounding verse is needed to identify the person intended. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 32 times across 31 verses, with most occurrences in Psalms. The name appears from 2 Samuel through Jeremiah, including passages in 2 Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, and Psalms.

This word refers to a builder or mason—someone whose work involves constructing walls or other masonry. Its basic meaning is “builder; mason,” and it functions as a noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Kings 12:13 and 2 Kings 22:6. These references show where the word appears, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the particular task or context in each passage.

This word refers to an estimate or valuation—the assessed worth assigned to something. As a noun, it names the amount or judgment used when something is valued, rather than describing the act of valuing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 27:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains an established estimate of worth.

The verb means “exalt oneself”: it describes a person raising himself up or claiming an elevated position. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its central idea is self-exaltation—directing honor or elevation toward oneself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, at Job 15:25. Its precise force there is best understood with the surrounding verse text.

This Greek verb means “pick,” describing the act of gathering or removing something, especially in wording connected with crops or fruit. It appears eleven times in the Greek Old Testament, across eleven verses, so its basic sense is consistent while the surrounding passage determines what is being picked. The word is found from Leviticus through Song of Songs and is also used in passages from Deuteronomy, Judges, 1 Samuel, Job, and Hosea. Its meaning is an action rather than a person, object, or quality.

ὑπερκεράω means “outflank” or “attack the wings of”—a verb describing a tactical move against the side of an opposing force. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 7:46. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, but without the verse text, the specific military situation cannot be described further. Its basic sense is a deliberate maneuver intended to gain advantage by striking around an enemy’s flank.

Phalaia, also rendered Falea, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 3:24. Since it is a proper name, its role is to identify a person in the genealogy rather than communicate a broader concept by itself. The surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific place in that family record.

This noun refers to a certain person—an individual who is not further identified by name. It is a general designation rather than a personal name, allowing someone to be mentioned without specifying exactly who he is. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 8:13. The precise role it carries in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains “certain person.”

This Greek LXX verb means “sentinel; guard”: it describes watching over or protecting something as a guard would. It presents guarding as an active duty rather than merely being present. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Wisdom 17:15. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic sense is the attentive work of keeping watch and providing protection.

Charman or Kharman is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament text preserved in the Septuagint. It is rendered “Charman” in the available English translation, while “Kharman” is another form of the same name. It occurs once, at Ezekiel 27:23, so its exact identity or role must be determined from that passage. It is not a common descriptive word or action; it functions as a name.

Chet, also rendered Khet, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a named figure or group connected with the ancestral account in Genesis. The name appears 11 times, all in Genesis, from Genesis 23:3 through Genesis 49:32. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a personal or group name.

This noun means “dust” or “chaff”—light, insubstantial material that can be scattered or blown away. It describes something lacking weight or lasting stability, whether referring to fine particles of earth or the dry husks separated from grain. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, the word occurs six times: five times in Old Testament passages and once in Wisdom. Its use in Psalms, Isaiah, Hosea, and Wisdom consistently presents dust or chaff as something fleeting and easily dispersed.

This noun means “pair of scissors,” referring to a cutting tool rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within Exodus, so its use is specific and concrete. The word names a physical implement used for cutting, not the act of cutting itself. Its meaning remains focused on this ordinary tool wherever it appears.
